group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 61-year-old woman was evaluated late this morning in the surgical optimization clinic three days before a planned open left lateral segmentectomy for a 3-cm colorectal liver metastasis discovered on routine surveillance; the hepatobiliary team anticipates a long right subcostal incision with possible extension across the midline, approximately four hours of operative time, low central venous pressure guidance to limit blood loss that is nonetheless expected to approach 600 mL, and a postoperative course beginning in the step-down unit for overnight hemodynamic monitoring before transfer to the general ward. She arrived having driven herself from a neighboring town, walked briskly from the parking deck up one flight of stairs and along the atrium corridor without pausing, and greeted the receptionist conversationally. At home she cooks, gardens, and walks her dog on a half-mile loop that includes a modest hill, reporting that knee soreness—not breathlessness—dictates her pace. Nine years ago she experienced crushing substernal discomfort while vacuuming; emergency coronary angiography revealed an occlusion of the distal right coronary artery that was treated with a drug-eluting stent, and repeat imaging two years later showed patent stent and non-obstructive lesions elsewhere. Since the infarction she has had no chest pain, follows cardiology twice yearly, and completed a symptom-limited Bruce treadmill test last autumn that reached eight metabolic equivalents without ischemic electrocardiographic changes. Medications include aspirin 81 mg each morning, clopidogrel 75 mg daily scheduled to be stopped five days pre-op per cardiology, metoprolol succinate 50 mg at breakfast, losartan 25 mg daily, and rosuvastatin 20 mg at night. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed during an employment physical four years ago; glycated hemoglobin at that time was 7.1 %, and she has since maintained values between 6.6 % and 7.2 % on metformin extended-release 1000 mg nightly and diet counseling alone, with home glucometer readings typically 95–130 mg/dL fasting and no hypoglycemia. She denies ever using injectable glucose-lowering therapy. Additional history includes well-controlled primary hypertension for which lisinopril was recently switched to losartan because of cough, cholelithiasis managed expectantly, seasonal allergic rhinitis, and remote laparoscopic appendectomy at age 22. There is no personal history of stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid surgery, seizure disorder, peripheral arterial disease, chronic lung disease, or kidney stones. She quit cigarette smoking 18 years ago after an 8-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of chardonnay with Saturday dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Her mother succumbed to myocardial infarction at 79, and her father died of colon cancer at 83; no siblings have cardiovascular disease before 65. Review of systems today is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, palpitations, presyncope, claudication, abdominal pain other than occasional right upper-quadrant twinges when bending, change in bowel habits, dysuria, fevers, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. After five minutes of quiet sitting, vital signs obtained in the right arm measured blood pressure 118/64 mm Hg, regular pulse 62 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oral temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air; height is 165 cm, weight 71 kg, and body-mass index 26 kg/m². She appears well nourished and in no acute distress; conjunctiva are pink, sclera anicteric, and skin warm without diaphoresis. Neck veins are not distended at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line with normal amplitude. Heart sounds reveal a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2 with no gallop, click, or murmur. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation throughout with full diaphragmatic excursion. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, and mildly tender deep in the right upper quadrant over the palpable edge of segment III of the liver; no guarding, rebound, or ascites is present, and bowel sounds are normoactive. Extremities are warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally, and no edema or cyanosis. Neurologic screening shows full orientation, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all muscle groups, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Airway examination demonstrates a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor gap 4 cm, thyromental distance 6.5 cm, full cervical range of motion, and good dentition. Laboratory data drawn one hour before the visit reveal hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, white blood cells 6.8 ×10⁹/L, platelets 248 ×10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.91 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate over 80 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting glucose in the same specimen is 118 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 26 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 85 U/L, and international normalized ratio 1.0. Twelve-lead electrocardiography obtained today displays normal sinus rhythm at 60 beats/min, inferior Q waves consistent with the prior infarction, and no acute ST-T changes relative to a tracing six months ago. Upright postero-anterior chest radiograph shows clear lung fields and an unremarkable cardiomediastinal silhouette. The anesthetic plan reviewed with her includes balanced general anesthesia with low central venous pressure strategy, arterial line and large-bore peripheral access for real-time hemodynamic monitoring, epidural catheter placement for postoperative analgesia provided coagulation parameters remain stable, continuation of beta-blocker and metformin on the morning of surgery, withholding clopidogrel as scheduled, point-of-care glucose checks every two hours intra-operatively, judicious crystalloid limited to 2 mL/kg/h until resection margins are secured, cell-saver autotransfusion readiness in the event of higher blood loss, and sequential compression sleeves with postoperative pneumatic compression transitioning to low-dose subcutaneous heparin once epidural removal criteria are satisfied. After a thorough discussion covering bleeding, biliary leak, deep venous thrombosis, myocardial events, pulmonary complications, wound infection, and the necessity for early mobilization, she summarized back medication timing and fasting instructions accurately and voiced understanding as well as willingness to proceed with the scheduled liver resection.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative risk factors:
- High-risk surgery: Open liver segmentectomy is intraperitoneal surgery → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: Her prior myocardial infarction qualifies despite a subsequent negative stress test → 1.
- History of heart failure: None reported → 0.
- History of stroke or TIA: Neither reported → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: Diabetes is managed with metformin and diet, not insulin → 0.
- Creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: Preoperative creatinine is 0.91 mg/dL → 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
